title: Victoria Street North towers and Grand River Rocks displacement
subtitle: Affordable housing, public plaza, parking, construction impacts on a neighbouring restaurant, and planning deadline pressures
overview: The committee held a public meeting on a proposal to redevelop 236-264 Victoria Street North with two towers of up to 40 storeys. Staff recommended approving the Official Plan and zoning changes, along with an urban design report. The site is currently zoned for up to eight storeys.

The committee did not vote on the staff recommendation. It recommended referring the matter to the Council meeting held later the same day {{vote:m1}}. The aim is to give the applicant time to supply information on affordable housing and to address concerns from Grand River Rocks, a climbing gym that has leased space on the site.

This matters to residents because the project would add roughly 1,000 homes near transit but currently includes no affordable units. It would also displace a well-used community business. A planning-law deadline means the application must be decided by April 19. After that date, part of the application fee must be refunded and the applicant can appeal for lack of a decision. Staff said they would also contact a neighbouring restaurant about construction impacts. Council will decide the matter.

decisions.detail: The committee recommended that Council take up the staff recommendation on the Official Plan amendment, zoning amendment and urban design report for 236-264 Victoria Street North at its meeting later that day, so the applicant has time to provide affordable housing information and address Grand River Rocks' concerns {{vote:m1}}.

debate: Delegates from Grand River Rocks and many members described the gym as a community hub, including camps and children's programs. They said the climbing walls are built for the specific space and need about ten years of operation to recover costs. They asked for the approval to be denied or delayed so the lease could run its full term.

Councillors asked about the lease terms, noting that a lease termination clause favours the landlord. One councillor said the committee could only weigh planning merits, and that a refusal could be appealed to the Ontario Land Tribunal. Staff said an appeal would likely cost over $100,000, and that applicants have mostly won such appeals.

Several councillors pressed on affordable housing. The applicant's planner said the site is outside a major transit station area, so inclusionary zoning does not apply. The planner said the owner has made no commitment but is not closing the door. Councillors also asked for green space in the public plaza and for a lower parking ratio.

The applicant's planner said the site is not ready to build, citing site contamination review, rail agreements with Metrolinx and CN, and market uncertainty. The planner estimated a building permit application could be about five years away and said the owner was open to talking with the gym. Some councillors said it was not possible to build around the existing gym building.

The owner of a neighbouring restaurant supported the project but asked for reasonable notice of utility shutoffs and less road blockage during construction. Staff said the site plan process requires a construction and parking phasing plan. Some councillors also objected to being pushed by the 120-day decision deadline.
